items.title: Charles McPherson interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He did make a record with Yusef Lateef... And we were recommended by Yusef, who worked with Mingus sometimes

ctx.x: The name Lonnie Hillyer comes up.

Yeah. Lonnie lived right on my street. He’s about almost a year younger. He died in 1985. Very, very talented. Very, you know he’s one of these guys that you always read about, you always read about this prototype talented person, died young, no one knew who in the heck he was. I mean there are of course — some musicians know. But he never got any recognition, he never was involved in any real say visible records. He did © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

make a record with Yusef Lateef, he might have been involved with James Moody on a record or something like that, but he never, he was kind of a tragic figure. He never just got his just due and he wasn’t around long enough. And then, it’s kind of sad. But anyway he was my best friend. Very talented. Very, very talented. And he just died in 1985, a young man. He was about 45. It was just one of those things. We went to New York together, as far as working with Mingus, yes. Yeah, we worked, let’s see this was…

items.title: Yusef Lateef — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: he taught uh the saxophonist Charles McPherson, from about age 13 somewhere

ctx.x: Uh could you talk about your um, your stints working with uh, with Barry Harris?

Oh, yes. Barry Harris is, is respected, highly respected, particularly in Detroit when we were all there, they called him the “high priest of music.” Um...he taught uh the saxophonist Charles McPherson, from about age 13 somewhere, and Lonnie Hilliyer. He’s a very wise man. In fact, I think I learned more about autophysiopsychic music from Barry than other one person, and he’s, he’s a world teacher right today. I respect him highly.
